title: Why Did the Concorde Drop Its Nose?
description:
Every time Concorde landed, its whole nose bent down, like a bird lowering its beak. It looked strange, almost alive, and it was not for show. Without that bend, the pilots could not have seen the runway. Concorde was full of parts like that, a glass shield over the windows, a wheel under the tail, fuel that moved around in flight. Today, ten parts of the fastest airliner ever to carry passengers in regular service, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:23 1. The nose that bends
2:49 2. The glass shield
4:12 3. The wing with no flaps
5:36 4. The wheel under the tail
6:51 5. The engine intakes
8:12 6. The afterburners
9:27 7. The fuel that moved
10:42 8. The tiny windows
11:51 9. The white paint
13:15 10. The carbon brakes
14:45 The verdict

Sources:
- Concorde general (first flight 2 Mar 1969, reheat Mach 0.95-1.7, digital intake control, fuel trim, small windows, tail wheels ~18 deg, Dunlop carbon brakes, AF4590 and Kevlar liners): Wikipedia, "Concorde" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concorde
- Nose droop 5 / 12.5 deg, 6-8 in stretch, 120 C skin, 60,000 ft, speeds, 3 h 6 min crossing, 5,000 h wind tunnel: AIN, "Concorde facts" https://oldain.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2012-07-11/concorde-facts
- Visor (letter-box quote, glazed visor, gold film, gear interlock, manual nose release): Heritage Concorde https://heritageconcorde.com/nose-and-visor-general
- Pepsi Concorde 1996, Mach 2 limited to 20 minutes: General Aviation News https://generalaviationnews.com/2024/08/28/supersonic-soda-for-cola-concorde/
